name: Cardiogen

lead: Cardiogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as acting on cardiovascular tissue. In longevity circles it is discussed for organ rejuvenation and healthier aging.

It is reported to stimulate proliferation in heart-tissue cultures, lower the pro-apoptotic protein p53 and interact with DNA and histones. In old rats it was reported to inhibit growth of a transplanted M-1 sarcoma. The literature is limited to organotypic cultures and rats; no human studies were found and no appearance use is documented.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course organ-bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any effect is a hope tied to heart health and aging rather than to looks directly.
No human safety data exist, and it is not approved for therapeutic use.

angle.text: Cardiogen is a short peptide aimed at heart tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging peptide for healthier aging. Data are sparse rat and cell studies with no human trials; no appearance link is known.

lead: Cardiogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide, Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg (AEDR), of about 489 daltons, developed in the research program of Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and described as a cardiovascular-targeted bioregulator [1][2]. It is discussed within the wider anti-aging peptide field, where people interested in healthy ageing and a younger-looking body follow the Khavinson bioregulators [2].

Reported work is limited to organotypic cultures, cell lines and rats, including stimulation of proliferation in heart tissue explants from young and old animals, reduced p53 expression, and dose-dependent inhibition of transplanted M-1 sarcoma growth in senescent rats [1][3]. Reports of smaller heart-attack damage in rats come from a patent and are not directly confirmed by peer-reviewed literature, according to the Grokipedia summary [1]. Cardiogen is not approved for human therapeutic use and is sold as a research chemical [1].
infobox: Not approved for human therapeutic use [1]

paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946 to 2024) directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and promoted peptide bioregulators as geroprotectors; Wikipedia lists organ-derived preparations such as Thymalin and Epithalamin approved in Russia and the CIS, along with shorter synthetic peptides, though its article does not mention Cardiogen [2]. Wikipedia notes that its account relies largely on his own publications and carries a promotional-content banner [2].

An AI-generated encyclopedia summary reports that Cardiogen increased proliferation in rat heart explants from young and old animals, reduced p53, raised cytoskeletal proteins 2 to 5 times in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, and binds DNA and histones [1]. In senescent rats with transplanted M-1 sarcoma, Cardiogen injections raised tumour-cell apoptosis and inhibited tumour growth in a dose-dependent manner via haemorrhagic necrosis and apoptosis, according to the study abstract [3]. The same summary links the peptide to senescence-related cardiac impairment as a hypothesis [1].
No regulatory approval and no registered human clinical trials exist, according to the Grokipedia summary, and suppliers sell it as a research chemical disclaiming human use [1].
No studies found. Laboratory and rat research is described above [1][3].
